text: The second shift ended twenty minutes ago and I am still sitting in the car in the lot with the keys in my hand. The steering wheel is cold and I have not turned the engine on. My eyes close on their own and I let them for a count of ten.

The baby went down at four and is up at five and I am standing at the crib with my eyes half shut, swaying from habit. My arms are lead from the shoulder down. The clock says a number I decide not to read.

Nine hours on the interstate and the last exit is still forty miles off and the coffee stopped working around hour six. I crack the window and the cold does nothing. My hands are at ten and two because I no longer trust them anywhere else.

I have turned him in the bed and changed the sheets and given the pills and it is only two in the afternoon. The chair by his bed has my shape in it now. I sit back down and the ceiling swims a little and I let it.

Forty essays are graded and twenty-two are not and the red pen has started to feel heavy. I read the same paragraph three times and it does not go in. The kitchen clock has stopped making sense and the tea is cold.

The truck is unloaded and the boxes are in rooms that are roughly right and the mattress is on the floor. I lie down on it in my shoes. Every joint has its own small complaint and I listen to none of them.
The last mile of the trail is all downhill and my knees have stopped cushioning anything. Each step lands and I feel it in my teeth. The parking lot is a rumor somewhere below the trees.

It is the third night in the chair beside the hospital bed and the chair has stopped pretending to be comfortable. The monitor beeps on a rhythm I know in my sleep now. I rest my forehead on the bed rail and the metal is cool.

The last table left at eleven and the floor is mopped and the chairs are up and my feet have gone past hurting into something flat. I count the drawer twice because the first count did not stick. The walk to the bus stop is four blocks and I think about each one.

The plane lands at six in the morning in a city where my body thinks it is midnight and the line for customs folds back on itself nine times. I shuffle forward with the bag strap cutting into my shoulder. My face feels like it belongs to someone who has been awake longer than me.
The last bin of apples is on the trailer and the light is going and my hands have stopped closing all the way. I lean on the tailgate. The rows I picked today look the same as the rows I have not.

Three exams in two days and the fourth is tomorrow and the textbook pages have begun to slide past without leaving anything behind. I am reading with my chin in my hand and my hand is losing. The library lights buzz and I could sleep under them.

The train home is standing room only and I am leaning against the pole with my eyes closed and my bag between my feet. Every stop the doors open and the cold comes in and I do not move. The week has had eleven days in it.

It is the ninth hour on the register two days before the holiday and the line has not been shorter than twelve since noon. I say the same four sentences and my mouth does them without me. My lower back has become a single dull note.

The dish pit is finally empty at one in the morning and my hands are white and wrinkled to the wrist. I peel off the gloves and they come away like a second skin. The bus does not run this late and the walk is uphill.

I have read the bedtime book twice and sung the song three times and he is still asking for water. My voice has gone flat and I can hear it. I sit on the floor by the bed because standing up again seems like a lot to ask.

Six hours in the waiting room and the number on the screen has moved eleven places. The chair has no back that my back recognizes. I have read every poster twice and the vending machine has nothing left I want.

The fifth interview of the day is at four and I am in the lobby in the same suit, smoothing the same folder. My face has smiled so much it feels borrowed. I say my name to the receptionist and it sounds like a word I am still learning.

The kitchen has been a construction site for four months and tonight I am washing dishes in the bathtub again with sawdust in my hair. The microwave is on the floor of the living room. I dry a plate and sit down on the edge of the tub with it in my lap.

Mile twenty-two and my legs are running on something other than me and the crowd noise has gone far away. Each stride is a negotiation. I keep my eyes on the back of the runner ahead because looking further is more than I can do.

A week of two-hour nights and the words on the screen have started to drift when I stop looking directly at them. I type a sentence and read it back and it is not a sentence. My eyes are sand and the blinking does not help.
The calves are fed and the gate is fixed and the tractor is under the roof and it is dark and I am still in the yard. My boots weigh what they weigh. The porch light is a long way across the gravel.

Twelve hours on the ward and the handover is done and I am sitting in the break room with my shoes off and my feet on the opposite chair. The coffee pot has a quarter inch of something in it. I look at it and decide it is too far.

Six hundred miles today and the truck stop lights are too bright and the shower token is in my pocket and I cannot make myself walk to the building. I sit in the cab with the engine ticking. The next load picks up at five.

The twins are finally asleep at the same time for the first time today and I am lying on the floor between the cribs because that is where I was standing. The carpet is fine. The monitor light blinks green and I watch it blink.

Day three of the conference and the badge lanyard has worn a groove in my neck and the talks have merged into one long slide. I am in the back row with my coat on. Someone asks a question and I nod at it from very far away.

The last relative has driven off and the turkey carcass is in a bag and the table is a field of crumpled napkins. I sit at the end of it with my apron still on. The dishwasher is full and the sink is full and I will get to them.

The week of the funeral is over and the casseroles are stacked in the freezer and the thank-you cards are in a pile I cannot look at. I sit on the stairs with my coat half off. Every part of me is heavy in a way that sleep did not touch.

The release went out at four in the morning and the bugs came in at six and I am looking at a stack trace with my cheek on my fist. The keyboard has a wet spot where my coffee was. My thoughts arrive one at a time and slowly.

Seven meetings back to back and the last one ran long and my voice has gone to gravel. I close the laptop and the room is suddenly very quiet. My shoulders will not come down from where they have been all day.

The last box comes off the truck and my back makes a sound and I set it down wherever it lands. The stairs to the third floor are behind me forty times. I lean against the doorframe and the doorframe does most of the work.

The driveway is shoveled for the second time today, after work, in the dark, and the plow has already pushed a new wall across the end of it. I stand with the shovel upright like a flag. My arms hang and the snow keeps coming.

The third feed of the night and I am in the rocking chair with the bottle at an angle and my head against the wall. The night light makes the room orange. I count her swallows to stay awake and lose count.

Friday at three fifteen and the last class has gone and I am sitting at my desk with twenty-eight chairs in front of me, all empty, all crooked. The whiteboard still has the morning's problem on it. I do not have it in me to erase it yet.

The billable day ended at nine and I am still at the desk with the file open and the words not landing. The building is silent except for the vacuum somewhere below. I put my glasses on the desk and press my palms into my eyes.

Call number one hundred and six and the script is coming out of me without my hearing it anymore. The headset has worn the top of my ear raw. The clock on the wall is a thing I have stopped believing in.

The ferry is two hours late and the terminal benches are steel and the kids have run out of everything, including the will to complain. I am holding the sleeping one and the other is leaning on my knee. My arm went numb a while ago and I have left it that way.

The laundry is a mountain on the bed and the mountain has to be moved before anyone can sleep in the bed. I fold one shirt and sit down on the corner. The shirt is in my lap and the rest of the mountain is where it was.

It is eleven at night and raining and the dog has to go out and I am standing under the streetlight in a coat over pajamas holding the leash. He takes his time. I lean on the lamppost and the lamppost holds.

The last guest is gone and the tent is still up and the rented glasses are in crates and I am sitting in a folding chair in the middle of the lawn. My shoes are off beside me and the dew is coming up. The lights are still on in the trees and I do not have the arms to take them down.
Fourteen hours on and the bus home is warm and I am fighting to keep my head from going against the window. It goes against the window. The stop announcements come from somewhere underwater.

The defense is over and the committee has shaken my hand and I am in the hallway with my laptop bag and nowhere to put myself. Five years landed in two hours. I sit on the floor against the lockers because the floor is there.

The warehouse shift ends at six in the morning and the sky outside the dock door is going gray and my scanner hand has a claw shape it will not let go of. I punch out and stand by the time clock. The parking lot is a long bright rectangle.

The flight is canceled and the next one is at seven and the airport chairs have armrests designed to keep anyone from lying down. I have found a square of carpet by a gate that is not in use. My coat is my pillow and the announcements are my lullaby.

I have visited the care home every day for three weeks and today she did not know my name and I drove home anyway and here I am in the garage with the engine off. The door into the house is six feet away. I will open it in a minute.

The planting is done, four hundred seedlings, and my back will not straighten past a certain angle and I have stopped asking it to. I walk to the truck bent like a question mark. The water jug is empty and the sun is still up.

The toddler has been sick for five days and I have been awake for most of them and the pediatrician's hold music is the quietest thing I have heard all week. I sit on the bathroom floor with the phone on speaker. The tile is cool and I lie down on it.

The overnight bakery shift is done and the trays are washed and the sun is coming up as I walk home against the commuter traffic. Flour is in the creases of my knuckles. My bed is four blocks away and I am measuring them.

The inventory count is finished at two in the morning and every number on the clipboard has been checked twice and I no longer know what the numbers are for. The store lights hum. I sit on a pallet of dog food and look at the floor.

The deadline passed at midnight and the thing was sent and now it is one and I am sitting in front of the screen with nothing left to do and no idea how to stop. My hands are still on the keys. The cursor blinks at me in an empty document.

The potty training day ended with the seventh pair of pants in the wash and I am on the couch with the baby monitor and a glass of water I have not drunk. The television is on with the sound off. My eyelids have their own schedule.

The long drive back from the funeral ends in my own driveway at midnight and I sit there with the headlights on the garage door. The suit is wrinkled into me. I turn the key and the sudden quiet is almost too much to carry inside.

The sixth bedtime trip up the stairs and I am climbing them with my hand on the wall. He wants the door open a different amount. I adjust the door and sit on the top step in the dark and do not go down.

The harvest crew has gone and the combine is parked and I am in the kitchen with my boots off and my socks black with dust. The soup is on the stove and I do not get up to stir it. My arms rest on the table like things someone left there.

The last patient note is typed at eight and the clinic is dark and I am walking to the car through a lot that seems to have grown. My keys are heavier than keys. I get in and sit with the door open and one foot still on the pavement.

Mile three of the walk home with the dead phone and the broken-down car behind me and the shoes that were never meant for this. My heels are raw and I have stopped adjusting my stride around it. The streetlights go on one by one ahead of me and each one is farther than the last.
